$comment: Rules and baseline for eng-tools/check-secrets.mjs: the identifiers no entropy scanner
recognises. gitleaks covers the credential classes and is configured in .gitleaks.toml.
The rules below are armed with THIS deployment's values, because development happens in this
repository now and nothing upstream of it strips an identifier any more. A digest discloses
nothing; the domain is a company domain, not a secret, and it is the string that must never
appear. A fork should replace both with its own — or empty them, which disarms the rule.
decided what its own deployment must not disclose. To arm a rule:
aws-account-id     add the SHA-256 of your account id to `digests` — never the id itself,
internal-hostname  add `"domain": "<your-domain>"`; with none, the rule never fires
`pending` is a ratchet, not an allowlist: it records what the tree carried when the gate was
armed, the gate fails when a count grows or a file not named here acquires one, and
`pnpm run check:secrets -- --write-baseline` can only ever shrink it.

aws-account-id.why: A 12-digit account id in an ARN tells a reader which account to enumerate.
aws-account-id.matches: every 12-digit run, compared by SHA-256 so this file carries no literal

internal-hostname.why: Per-environment hostnames name endpoints that are not part of the published surface.
internal-hostname.matches: any subdomain of `domain` below; no rule fires when it is absent

aws-resource-id.why: A VPC, subnet or security-group id is the network topology of a live deployment.
aws-resource-id.matches: vpc- subnet- sg- igw- rtb- acl- eni- ami- vol- snap- followed by 8 or 17 hex digits
aws-resource-id.redacts-to: <prefix>-EXAMPLE — not a hex body, which would still match this rule

internal-tracker.why: A tracker URL cites a record an outside reader cannot open, and names our instance.
internal-tracker.redacts-to: nothing — the citing prose has to be rewritten by a human, so the export fails instead
